Rhodium-Catalyzed Trifluoromethoxylation of Allenylic
Trichloroacetimidates
Yangdong Hou,* Yicheng Luo, and Pingping Tang*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 9764−9768
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The first rhodium-catalyzed trifluoromethoxylation of allenylic trichloroacetimidates has been reported. The products
were obtained through a procedure using trifluoromethyl arylsulfonate (TFMS) as the trifluoromethoxy source with a yield up to
76% by identifying the ligand of diene. The reaction proceeds under mild reaction conditions with excellent functional group
tolerance and complete regiocontrol.
F
luorinated compounds are receiving increasing attention
because the introduction of a fluorinated functional group
into compounds can significantly influence their lipophilicity,
which is extremely important in drug molecules, pesticides, and
materials.
1
In particular, the OCF
3
group has one of the
highest lipophilicity values (π
x
= 1.04) compared to those of
CF
3
(π
x
= 0.88) and SO
2
CF
3
(π
x
= 0.55). Therefore, the
unique peculiarity of trifluoromethoxy intrigues chemists to
develop catalytic methods for efficient synthesis of trifluor-
omethoxylated molecules.
2
However, due to the easy
decomposition of trifluoromethoxy into difluorophosgene
and fluoride as well as β-fluoride elimination from transition-
metal-trifluoromethoxide complexes, introducing this func-
tional group remains a major challenge, especially the site-
selective trifluoromethoxylation on a precise molecule.
3
Allenes exist in many natural products and pharmaceuticals.
4
The uniqueness that accumulated double bonds along with
high activity make it widely used as synthons for cyclization,
5
hydrogenheteroatom reactions,
6
and multifunctionalization.
7
The versatile reactivity of allenes allows for the selective
modification of different positions, enabling the synthesis of
highly functionalized compounds.
8
Palladium catalysts were
used to catalyze the conversion of allenylic derivatives. The
palladium intermediate is attacked via an outer-sphere pathway
using soft nucleophiles.
9
When using hard nucleophiles, the
1,3-dienes are obtained through an inner-sphere pathway.
10
Nevertheless, the reactions that structurally maintain allene are
much less explored. Ma and co-workers reported palladium
catalyzed various conversions of α-centra carbon of allenes.
11
Carreira’s group achieved various functionalization of allenylic
carbonates using iridium catalysts (Scheme 1a).
12
However,
the functionalization of α-centra fluorinated allenes has not yet
been reported. Given some of our previous work,
13
we are
greatly encouraged to explore the trifluoromethoxy substitu-
tion reaction of α-centra secondary carbon in allenes. Herein,
we report our efforts to develop the first trifluoromethoxy
substitution reaction of allenylic trichloroacetimidates using a
Rh catalyst (Scheme 1b).
Different leaving groups significantly affect the activity of the
substrates. We began our studies by choosing the alkyl
secondary allenylic ester as the model substrate, which showed
high stability that can be recovered completely (See Table S1
in the Supporting Information). Certainly, we attempted to use
Pd and Ir for trifluoromethoxylation of allenylic esters but
failed (see Table S1 in the Supporting Information).

Trichloroacetimidate is a good leaving group and normally
used in the synthesis of glycosides.
14
Moreover, Nguyen and
co-workers achieved amination of allylic trichloroacetimidate
using rhodium catalyst.
15
Ultimately, by switching the leaving
group from Ac and Boc to trichloroacetimidate, a slight yield of
8% was finally obtained (entry 1 in Table 1). Silver salts were
added to activate the catalyst by removing the chlorine.
16
As
expected, a yield of 36% was furnished with 0.3 equiv of AgF
(entry 2). Lowering the reaction temperature to −40 °C
resulted in a slight increase in the yield (entry 3). After
screening the equivalent of AgF, a yield of 49% was achieved
using 0.5 equiv of AgF as an additive (entry 5). Other silver
salts can lead to a slight decrease in yield (entries 7 to 9). The
yield ascends to 58% with TBABF
4
as a phase transfer catalyst
(entry 11). Replacing the diene ligand of rhodium from
cyclooctadiene to L1 delivered a slight increase in yield with
62% similar to L3 (entry 13 and 15), while the use of electron-
rich diene L2 resulted in a decrease in the yield (entry 14).
The other ligands L4 and L5 afforded almost no product. It is
worth noting that the reaction proceeded with completely
regiocontrol.
With the optimized condition in hand (entry 13 in Table 1),
we began to examine the scope of allenylic trichloroacetimi-
dates (Scheme 2). Generally, both electron-donating and
electron-withdrawing groups including OMe, CF
3
, and NO
2
were well tolerated, providing the corresponding products in
60−62% yields (3a−3c). Substrates that contain halogen can
be applied to this system, which allowed further decoration
(53−65%, for 3d and 3e). However, the sulfonamide substrate
provided the product with a higher yield (70%, 3f), probably
due to the coordination of sulfone. Substrates bearing

functional groups near the allenylic site afforded medium yields
(45−55%, 3g and 3h). In addition, compared with 3a, the
yield of 3i increased to 67%, which may be due to the greater
electron-withdrawing effect of the ester group. Besides the
ester group, ether can also be a connecting motif, which is
helpful to introduce more different groups into the substrates
and greatly enrich the diversity of products (46−49%, 3j and
3k). This method also worked well with the allylic group, and
the products were isolated with moderate yield (3k and 3m).
Notably, the alkyne can also be compatible with this catalytic
system (3l) in 50% yield. To our delight, heterocyclic
substrates can also be tolerated, affording the target products
in 52−76% yields (3n−3q). Since there are a lot of fluoride
anions in the system, silicon-containing groups probably will
not survive. Surprisingly, the steric hindered
t
BuPh
2
Si
remained and the target product was provided with a yield
of 42% (3r). Finally, we evaluated the potential of this catalytic
trifluoromethoxylation method for indole and its derivatives,
which delivered the corresponding product in 65% and 71%
yield, respectively. A gram-scale reaction was conducted, and
3n was prepared in 68% yield (Scheme 3).
Based on the related literature
15,17
and the recent work
18
by
our group, we suggest the mechanism shown in Scheme 4. It is
envisioned that a plausible mechanism would arise from
coordination of the nitrogen and the double bond of allenylic
trichloroacetimidate to the rhodium catalyst to form the
activated rhodium allenylic complex. Reductive elimination of
trifluoromethoxy should be a tough process as the most
favored β-fluoride elimination would take place from
transition-metal-trifluoromethoxide complexes. We consider
that the steric hindrance created by the ligands around the Rh
center would preclude the reaction of an external nucleophile
at C2; therefore, the favored reaction is observed to occur at
C4.
12a
This reaction proceeds with excellent regioselectivity,
which may be attributed to the outer-sphere mechanism of
attacking the C4.
In conclusion, we have presented the first example of
rhodium-catalyzed trifluoromethoxylation of allenylic trichlor-
oacetimidates using trifluoromethyl arylsulfonate (TFMS) as
an OCF
3
source. The combination of rhodium with diene
ligand exhibited excellent catalytic performance, providing a
range of allenylic trifluoromethoxy compounds with up to 76%
yield and complete regiocontrol, which are difficult to access
by other methods. Due to the easy decomposition of the OCF
3
group, carefully selecting the appropriate leaving group, ligand
structure, reaction temperature, solvent, and base was very
critical, as all the factors jointly guaranteed the smooth
transformation. This discovery also expanded the scope of the
application of trifluoromethoxy reagents.
